I’ll never forget how excited I was in 2006 when my first album sold 40,000 copies in its first week. I was 16 and couldn’t even fathom that that many people would care enough about my music to invest their time and energy into it. Since then I’ve tried to meet and thank as many people as I could who have given me the chance to chase this insane dream. Here we are all these years later and a hundred times that many people showed up for me this week. I have 4 million thank you’s I want to send to the fans, and 4 million reasons to feel even more proud of this album than I already was. Thank you for going out to celebrate this project in the movie theaters, investing in vinyl, streaming, watching the video, buying CDs, reading the poems I wrote inside the packaging, and immersing yourselves in The Life of a Showgirl. I’ll cherish this feeling forever. Just wow. Thank you for the lovely bouquet 💐 

📸: Mert Alas & Marcus Piggott

Brewing up new stars 🪄
 
@NASAWebb’s unique view of the stellar nursery known as NGC 7129 reveals numerous stars formerly hidden in this cosmic cauldron. 
 
Stars begin their life in cold, dense regions of dust and gas, hiding from view of most telescopes. Webb’s high degree of infrared sensitivity allows astronomers to peer through dust to study these baby stars. 
 
In this image, we can see stars in various stages of development. The most mature and massive (about 5-8x the mass of our Sun) is the region’s bright central star. In the cavity on the left, appearing in gold, is the largest demonstration of its impact. The outflows from an earlier stage in the star’s development carve into the dense molecular cloud of hydrogen, and combine with the star’s light, causing it to glow. 
 
The region on the right, represented in red, hides much younger objects than those on the left: protostars. As the protostars accumulate matter and increase mass, they eject outflows of super heated material that interact with matter around the star, creating shocks that cause the textured appearance we see in this image. More protostar outflows are at upper left where a dark shadow is being cast by a protostar disk, visible against the surrounding nebula, depicted in blue. 
 
Seeing these different structures help astronomers study the star lifecycle in various stages, leading to a more complete understanding of our universe. 

See more in the link in @NASAWebb’s bio.
 
Image credit: NASA, ESA, CSA, STScI, Processing: Alyssa Pagan.

A little luck and a lot of Grace go a long way (in this case, 250 miles up)!
 
Each crew’s zero-g indicator is unique. Ours, named Lucky, represents the golden dragon at the center of our Crew-13 patch, which honors the brave and resilient legacy of Apollo 13 on which we stand. 

Thinking of Crew-12 today, whose indicator is beginning to drop right about now as they re-enter Earth’s gravity!

We’re getting America underway on nuclear power in space and ushering in the era of a Nuclear NASA.

With the signing of an MOU with @energy, we’re taking the next giant leap toward exploring the outer solar system and sending American astronauts to Mars. Fission power will help us travel farther, operate longer, and power more capable scientific instruments.

There is so much packed into these photos. Unforgettable memories. Dragon has departed with Crew-12 and is on the way back to Earth after eight months. 

In front of Dragon is the antenna we installed together. These were both peak teamwork moments for @iss and ground teams across @nasa and commercial operators.

Moon-like Madagascar

An astronaut aboard the @Space_Station captured this photo of the Saririaky anorthosite massif in Madagascar. Anorthosite is a rock formed from magma that cools beneath Earth's surface and is made up of large mineral crystals.

They say when one door closes, another one opens. In this case, we are closing two doors and opening many more. I can’t wait to see what the future holds for Crew-12 reuniting with their families. The entire @iss crew wishes them a safe journey. Godspeed

Our microgravity indicator consists of four satellites orbiting a crocheted Earth, all hand-made elements by Jack’s daughter and my childhood best friend. Each crew member selected a personal symbol or “satellite.” A tether links each satellite to the Earth, representing our connection to our families, friends, and our one shared home. We’ll see this indicator drop as we re-enter Earth’s gravity tomorrow. 
 
I chose a panda holding a mushroom, two adorable symbols of environmental importance and cultural fascination. Pandas are modern icons of species preservation and international diplomacy, and a pivotal character in my childhood. Mushrooms, or fungi, are the great decomposers, with all life on earth depending on them to keep our soils healthy and food webs functioning. 
 
Jack chose a moon that his daughter hand-crocheted. Each color woven into the design represents a member of their family or a cherished shared activity. By bringing this piece with him, he keeps their bond close, allowing Jack to re-live happy memories while looking forward to the ones they’ll create when he returns.
 
Sophie chose a banana. Bananas are the world’s most common fruit, ordinary fruit shared by billions of people across every continent. Yet on orbit fresh fruit is rare. She wanted with us a playful reminder of kitchens and home—a familiar piece of Earth drifting weightless with us.
 
Andrey chose this thing, because it reminds me of an old space soviet movie. He would invite everyone to try to guess what this is.

And we present to you, Planet Gaia and her moons, floating here in Crew-12’s Dragon!

Warning: These slides may cause existential wonder ✨To celebrate World Space Week, today’s #GoogleDoodle spotlights a never-before-seen photo of the Rosebud Nebula – a cosmic stellar nursery located 3,300 light-years away, captured by the James Webb Telescope.  

Keep swiping for distant planets and cosmic phenomena, along with answers to a few of the millions of questions they spark  🌌

what is cosmic dust and how is it so thick|

Cosmic dust is a collection of tiny solid particles – microscopic grains of carbon, silicates, and ice – that float through outer space. Although they appear remarkably thick and solid, their apparent density is an illusion caused by immense scale.

Explore more with Google Search

why is jupiter’s north pole glowing electric blue|
 
Jupiter’s north pole glows electric blue because of a gigantic, permanent ultraviolet aurora caused by high-energy particles, gas excitation, and volcanic power.

what are the clouds in the carina nebula made of|

The clouds in the Carina Nebula are made of molecular gas and cosmic dust, with the main components being hydrogen, smaller amounts of ionized elements like oxygen, sulfur, and nitrogen – which give the nebula its colorful glow – and tiny grains of heavier elements like carbon and silicates.

how far away is our closest giant galactic neighbor, andromeda, and is it true it’s heading toward us| 

The Andromeda Galaxy is about 2.5 million light-years away from us, and it is indeed heading straight toward the Milky Way. Traveling at roughly 68 to 110 miles per second (110–180 km/s), the galaxies will collide and merge in about 4 to 4.5 billion years.

what are the massive bubbles that appear in space|

Massive bubbles in space are giant cavities or shells of hot, superthin gas carved out by exploding stars, stellar winds, or outbursts from supermassive black holes.

how can an ancient star cluster be made of “heavy metal”|

From the Moon to the 50-yard line.
 
Six months ago, @Astro_Christina flew @Eagles Super Bowl confetti around the Moon on the Artemis II mission. Yesterday, in a full circle moment, she served as honorary captain at an Eagles game, bringing a little Moon Joy to the field.
 
#ArtemisII #FlyEaglesFly #MoonJoy

At yesterday’s game, we had the honor of meeting record-setting Astronaut, Christina Koch, who was a part of the historic Artemis II mission that took place earlier this year. Eagles Cheerleader @meganlmckeon was so inspired by the mission, that she recently began a Masters Program in Planetary Sciences.

To commemorate a lifelong interest and her recent pursuit, Megan performed a solo that was a tribute to the Artemis II team, to ‘Fly Me to the Moon’ in her audition this past spring. Now six months later, she was able to meet Christina and share her admiration. Christina even presented Megan with a NASA Artemis II mission patch before the game!

A huge thank you to @astro_christina for coming out to the game and sharing in this moment, we’ll be cheering for you in all your future endeavors!🚀

Ancient beachcombing 🔎

This photo by our Perseverance rover shows the edge of an ancient Martian lake. By studying the rocks here, scientists can unlock clues to the area’s past water activity—as well as how the region could have supported life.

From Florida to the front door in under eight hours. 🚀

@nasa’s @spacex Crew-13 lifted off from Cape Canaveral, Florida, at 11:10 a.m. EDT on Oct. 1 aboard Dragon Grace. By 7:05 p.m. EDT, they had docked to the International Space Station: 7 hours, 55 minutes from launch to arrival, the fastest launch-to-docking by a U.S. spacecraft in station history.

But four spacefarers carried more than their own dreams into orbit.

“We carry with us on this journey all of you who have supported us along the way, and we hope to make you proud,” said mission commander Jessica Watkins shortly after reaching orbit.

For NASA astronaut Luke Delaney, CSA astronaut Joshua Kutryk, and Roscosmos cosmonaut Sergey Teteryatnikov, it was their first flight to space. For Watkins, her second. Together, they’ll conduct research to benefit life on Earth and advance exploration beyond it.

Lucky 13. A whole lot of Grace. One historic ride.

Relive the journey to their new home in orbit.

There’s no stopping us! NASA’s X-59 completes a record six flights in one week! We’re burning through the sky at a top speed of Mach 1.53, the X-59’s fastest speed to date! #NASA #Quesst #X59 #Supersonic

“…and to all of you down there on Earth and around Earth, we love you from the Moon.” - @astrovicglover 

When IKE said those words onboard Integrity as we watched the Earth setting behind the Moon, Christina, Jeremy, and I instantly knew he was honoring everyone on Earth as well as our friends in Low Earth Orbit. 

Six months ago, the four of us launched on Artemis II. Today, @nasa launched Jessica, Luke, Josh, and Sergey on Crew-13. We cheer those heroes and salute Soyuz MS-28, Crew-12, and Soyuz MS-29 all of whom have been in space during and following our mission. Human spaceflight is thriving in the golden age of exploration!!!

Godspeed, Crew-13. 🚀

On Thursday, Oct. 1, at 11:10 a.m. EDT (1510 UTC), four spacefarers embarked on their journey to the @ISS, where they will spend the next several months living, working, and conducting scientific research in low Earth orbit.

With their @SpaceX Dragon spacecraft scheduled to dock to the orbiting lab just under eight hours after liftoff, this flight marks the shortest-ever travel time for a U.S. spacecraft to the space station.
